content.jointProblem: What mechanisms cause fatigue cracking at AutomVoj’s painted mild-steel conveyor-frame welds in 2–6 °C cold stores, and could changes to welding procedure, filler material or joint geometry reduce crack initiation and growth? The first experiment should combine examination of failed joints with matched room-temperature and 2–6 °C cyclic-loading tests on representative joints, using measured service loads and controlled moisture conditions to test whether environmental exposure changes the failure mechanism.

rationale.text: Erić has directly relevant experimental experience investigating interactions between mechanical fatigue and thermal cycling in welded structural steel.

sources.quote: Four loading programmes were applied: isothermal fatigue at 20 °C, isothermal fatigue at −30 °C, in-phase thermo-mechanical fatigue (TMF), and out-of-phase TMF, with twelve specimens per programme.

rationale.text: His group has fatigue-testing, climate-chamber and finite-element resources relevant to designing a controlled reproduction study.

sources.quote: The group routinely uses servo-hydraulic fatigue testing machines, a climate chamber capable of reaching −60 °C, and in-house FE models

rationale.text: His field research provides a precedent for measuring operational loads and temperatures rather than relying only on workshop loading assumptions.

sources.quote: Operational load spectra were recorded by a data logger over an eight-month measurement campaign using strain gauges at twelve positions on two girders
Rainflow-counted stress spectra and simultaneous temperature records were used to construct a combined loading environment for assessment.

rationale.text: He has investigated weld residual stresses through measurements and simulations, providing a relevant approach for assessing whether fabrication-related stresses contribute to cracking.

sources.quote: Residual stresses in as-welded and post-weld heat-treated (PWHT) T-joint specimens of S460M low-alloy steel were measured by hole-drilling with strain-gauge rosettes
and compared with sequentially coupled thermal–mechanical FE simulations.

constraints.text: Test specimens must represent the actual painted mild-steel hollow-section connections, and the environmental comparison must include the reported 2–6 °C service range rather than substituting deep-subzero tests.

sources.quote: Our conveyor frames are welded from mild steel hollow section and painted for corrosion resistance before delivery.
weld joint cracking at the main crossmember-to-stringer connections

constraints.text: The investigation must account for the long service exposure and suspected combination of thermal cycling, condensation and belt-induced vibration; room-temperature load tests alone are not an adequate reproduction protocol.

Our suspicion is that the combination of thermal cycling, condensation, and the vibration load from loaded belts is doing something we are not seeing at ambient conditions.

constraints.text: Failure analysis must be planned around the two retained failed sections and existing site records, with specimen allocation agreed before destructive examination.

sources.quote: We have photos and measurements of the cracked joints from site visits, and we still have two of the failed sections in storage.

constraints.text: Combined low-temperature fatigue testing requires external facilities, and access to the researcher's shared chamber and fatigue machine must be reserved before committing to an extended campaign.

sources.quote: We do not currently have the equipment or know-how to test at low temperatures under cyclic load.
Erić's climate chamber and servo-hydraulic machine are shared with two other research groups; scheduling access for extended test campaigns requires advance coordination.

constraints.text: Company engineering effort must be explicitly allocated because development work competes with live projects and there is no dedicated R&D department.

sources.quote: We have no dedicated R&D department
our chief engineer and two senior automation engineers who allocate time between live projects and improvement work.

risks: There is a substantial transfer gap: the cited thermal-fatigue work uses specified structural steels, plate joints and much colder temperature excursions, whereas AutomVoj reports painted mild-steel hollow sections at 2–6 °C. The first experiment must test this transfer on representative joints; published temperature effects cannot be assumed to explain these failures.

Condensation-assisted corrosion, fabrication defects, local joint geometry and service loading could compete with or dominate temperature-related fatigue. The supplied research evidence does not establish a validated method for painted joints under condensation, and chamber humidity-control capability is unknown.

Two retained failed sections may not capture variability across the 14 replaced assemblies. Without representative service-load and environmental histories, accelerated tests could reproduce a different damage mechanism or fail to reproduce cracking.

Researcher availability, facility booking dates, project budget, company staff allocation and customer-site access remain unknown. Shared equipment and competing production work could delay a sufficiently representative campaign.

No service-life improvement is established for a changed weld procedure, filler or joint design; any proposed remedy would require comparison against baseline specimens and subsequent service validation.
questions: What are the exact steel grade, hollow-section dimensions, joint drawings, welding procedure, filler, inspection records and coating specification, and can matched unfailed joints and production-representative specimens be supplied?
Can the two failed sections be released for documented examination and selective destructive testing, and are failure locations, dates and operating histories available for all replaced assemblies?

Can customer conveyors be instrumented to measure weld-region strains or vibration, belt loads, start-stop events, temperature cycles, humidity and condensation, including defrost or washdown conditions?

Can the laboratory maintain stable 2–6 °C conditions with controlled humidity or condensation during cyclic loading, and accommodate representative connections and fixtures? If not, what additional equipment or partner laboratory is needed?
What researcher time and shared-equipment slots are available, who will lead the company work, and what budget and decision deadline can both parties commit to?

What evidence would justify adopting a change: agreement with observed fracture features, comparative fatigue results, manufacturability and coating compatibility, and what field-validation period is acceptable?
